title: But God Meant It for Good — Weeping, Forgiveness, Bones
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Today we read the last chapter of Genesis. Fifty chapters have brought us to this place — from "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" all the way down to a coffin standing in Egypt, unburied.
And before anything else today I want to ask one question: why is it that a man can be forgiven for seventeen years and still not dare to believe he has really been forgiven?
In chapter 50, verse 15, the moment their father is dead the brothers say at once, "It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him."

Seventeen years. They had lived together in Goshen, eaten together, kept the flocks together, carried their father to his grave together. And all that time they had privately assumed one thing: that Joseph was holding his hand only for their father's sake.
They had never once really believed that forgiveness.
1. He Went Up to Bury His Father
"Joseph fell on his father's face, wept on him, and kissed him." (Genesis 50:1)

"Fell on … face" is וַיִּפֹּל עַל־פְּנֵי (*vayipol al-penei*) in the Hebrew — the same movement as in chapter 45, when he threw his arms round Benjamin, and in chapter 46, when he threw his arms round his father.
This is the sixth time Joseph weeps in Genesis. Altogether he weeps seven times.

And the funeral that follows is staggering in scale: forty days for the embalming, and "The Egyptians wept for Israel for seventy days" — which is close to the scale of a state funeral for Pharaoh himself. Going up in the procession were "all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, all the elders of the land of Egypt" and "all the house of Joseph"; and "Both chariots and horsemen went up with him."
"It was a very great company" is הַמַּחֲנֶה כָּבֵד מְאֹד (*hamachaneh kaved me'od*) in the Hebrew — literally "the camp was exceedingly heavy", and "camp" is a military word.
Brothers and sisters, notice two details.

First: "Only their little ones, their flocks, and their herds, they left in the land of Goshen." — they left the children behind as a guarantee that they would certainly come back. And years afterwards, when Pharaoh wanted to stop Israel leaving Egypt, he used exactly the same move: "Go, but the children stay behind."
Second: Joseph is the vizier of Egypt, and yet he does not go to Pharaoh himself. He "spoke to Pharaoh's staff", and he even said, "If now I have found favor in your eyes."
A man who governs the whole of Egypt still speaks like a servant. The position went up; the posture did not change — and that is a very hard thing.

They went all the way up into Canaan, and at "the threshing floor of Atad" they lamented with a very great and severe lamentation, and mourned for seven days. Those seven days later became the fixed pattern of Jewish mourning.
And then: "His sons did to him just as he commanded them, for his sons carried him into the land of Canaan, and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah."
Twelve brothers, carrying their father together into that cave. It was the ground Abraham had bought — the only property this family held in the land of promise.
And the next sentence matters enormously: "Joseph returned into Egypt—he, and his brothers, and all that went up with him to bury his father, after he had buried his father." (Genesis 50:14)
They stood on the soil of the land of promise, and then they turned round and walked back. Because the time had not yet come.
The funeral was staged on that enormous scale, and yet he still says, "If now I have found favor in your eyes." What does that tell us?

He is the vizier who governs the whole of Egypt, and yet he does not go to Pharaoh himself. He "spoke to Pharaoh's staff", and he added a sentence on top of it: "If now I have found favor in your eyes." The position went up; the posture did not change — and that is a very hard thing to do. For most people the first thing that changes after a promotion is the way they speak: more commands and fewer requests, less explaining and more announcing. Joseph gives us a very practical test. To find out whether you have changed, don't consult what you feel inside; listen to the shape of the sentences you used the last three times you gave somebody an instruction. A man who is still asking is still a servant, however high his rank has climbed.
They left the children in Goshen. How much weight does that detail carry?

"Only their little ones, their flocks, and their herds, they left in the land of Goshen" — they left the children behind as a guarantee that they would certainly come back. And years afterwards, when Pharaoh wanted to stop Israel leaving Egypt, he used exactly the same move: "Go, but the children stay behind." The same device — one time a pledge given freely, the other time a hostage held by force. That contrast is buried very deep in the text, and it carries a warning for us: the thing you leave behind in Egypt of your own free will today may turn out to be the very thing that keeps you from getting out tomorrow. People are not usually held by chains. They are held by what they themselves left there.
2. A Light from the Original: Am I in the Place of God?
The moment their father is dead, the brothers panic.
"When Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, 'It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.'" (Genesis 50:15)
"Hate us" is יִשְׂטְמֵנוּ (*yistemenu*) in the Hebrew — and chapter 27, where Esau "hated" Jacob, uses that same word.
"Will fully pay us back" is וְהָשֵׁב יָשִׁיב (*vehashev yashiv*), an emphatic construction: "he will certainly, doubly repay."
And then they did something. They did not go themselves; they "sent a message to Joseph", and they produced their father's dying command: "Your father commanded before he died, saying …"
A great many interpreters think that dying command was very probably invented on the spot — the text nowhere records Jacob ever saying it.
They even reached for the heaviest word of all: "Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin."
"Forgive" is שָׂא נָא (*sa na*) in the Hebrew, literally "please lift it up, please carry it away." In Hebrew, to forgive is to shoulder something.
"Disobedience" is פֶּשַׁע (*pesha*), the heaviest of the three Hebrew words for sin — rebellion, treason; and "sin" is חַטָּאת (*chatat*), whose root meaning is "to miss the mark."
They said the whole thing, and they said it properly. But they said it through a messenger.
"Joseph wept when they spoke to him." (Genesis 50:17)
This is the seventh time he weeps, and the last.

Because it has been seventeen years. He brought them down to Egypt, gave them the best of the land, provided for them, and the whole family has been living life side by side. And all that time they have privately believed that he was gritting his teeth for their father's sake.
Brothers and sisters, this is the pain of being misread. The love you gave away is taken for conditional patience — and that hurts.
Then: "His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, 'Behold, we are your servants.'"
This is the last fulfilment of that dream in chapter 37. And this time it is they themselves who say, "we are your servants."
Joseph's answer is the first summit of this chapter:
"Don't be afraid, for am I in the place of God?" (Genesis 50:19)
"Am I in the place of God?" — what the Hebrew is asking is, "Am I sitting in God's seat?"
Brothers and sisters, that one sentence says everything there is to say about what forgiveness actually is.

What is refusing to forgive, at bottom? It is my insisting on climbing into the judgement seat. I will pronounce him guilty. I will decide what the damages come to. I will decide when he may be let off.
And Joseph says: that seat is not mine.
So here is the definition of forgiveness: not that you were never in the wrong, but that the judgement seat is not mine, and I am not going to sit down in it.
Romans 12 says, "Don't seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God's wrath. For it is written, 'Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.'"

To let Jesus be King is to move that case out of my courtroom and into his. It is not that nothing will be pursued; it is that the judge has been changed — and that judge is a great deal fairer than I am.
Forgiven for seventeen years — why can they still not believe it?

Seventeen years. They had lived together in Goshen, eaten together, kept the flocks together, carried their father to his grave together. And the moment their father died, out it came: "It may be that Joseph will hate us." All that time they had privately assumed that Joseph was holding his hand only for their father's sake. What is more, they did not go themselves; they sent the message through someone else, and propped it up with a dying command the text never records. There are two lessons buried here. One is for the person who gives — when the love you gave away is taken for conditional patience, that hurts. And one is for the person who receives — refusing to believe that you have been pardoned is itself a form of unbelief.
"Am I in the place of God?" — how does that sentence say everything about forgiveness?

What the Hebrew is asking is, "Am I sitting in God's seat?" What is refusing to forgive, at bottom? It is my insisting on climbing into the judgement seat: I will pronounce him guilty, I will decide what the damages come to, I will decide when he may be let off. And Joseph says: that seat is not mine. So the definition of forgiveness is not that you were never in the wrong; it is that the judgement seat is not mine, and I am not going to sit down in it. Romans 12 says, "Don't seek revenge yourselves … Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay." To let Jesus be King is to move that case out of my courtroom and into his — to change judges, for one who is a great deal fairer than I am.
3. What You Meant, and What God Meant
And now comes the most famous verse in the whole of Genesis:
"As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today." (Genesis 50:20)
Take that verse in two halves.
The first half: "you meant evil against me." The Hebrew is חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה (*chashavtem alai ra'ah*) — "you devised evil against me."
Joseph does not say, "well, you didn't really mean it." He does not say, "it's all in the past, don't dwell on it." He does not say, "you had your own difficulties too."
He says: you meant evil against me. Evil is evil.
The second half: "but God meant it for good." The Hebrew uses the very same verb, חָשַׁב (*chashav*) — "but God devised it for good."
One and the same event, two intentions — and it is God's intention that stands.
Brothers and sisters, those two halves have to be said together.

Say only the first half and we stay inside the injury and never get out of it as long as we live. Say only the second half and it is cheap papering-over — it wipes away the offender's responsibility, and it tells the injured person that their pain does not count.
And there is something I want to say with the greatest possible seriousness: who says this sentence matters more than what the sentence says.
The speaker is the victim himself, and he is speaking twenty-two years later — after the pit, after being sold, after being falsely accused, after prison, after being forgotten.
This sentence has never been given to bystanders to stop a suffering person's mouth with.
If somebody is in the middle of the pain and you walk over and say, "God meant it for good" — that is not comfort. That is dismissal.

Remember what the Lord Jesus did at the tomb of Lazarus. He knew perfectly well that in a few minutes Lazarus would walk out; and yet the text says, "Jesus wept." He wept first, and afterwards he performed the miracle.
Sit with them first, and speak afterwards. That order cannot be reversed.
Then comes verse 21: "'Now therefore don't be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.' He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them."

"Spoke kindly to them" is, in the Hebrew, "he spoke to their heart" — וַיְדַבֵּר עַל־לִבָּם (*vaydaber al-libam*). That is precisely the phrase of chapter 34, and it is the phrase behind what God says in Hosea: "I will allure her … and speak tenderly to her" — literally, speak to her heart.
He does not simply announce a pardon. He walks over and speaks to their heart.
That is forgiveness made whole: the position is settled, and the feelings are cared for as well.
"God meant it for good" — may I use that sentence to comfort somebody else?

Be extremely careful. First, the verse has two halves and they must be said together. The first half is "you meant evil against me" — evil is evil, and Joseph never says "you didn't really mean it"; only then comes the second half, "but God meant it for good", and the Hebrew uses the very same verb for both. Say only the first half and a person is left standing inside the injury with no way out; say only the second half and it is cheap papering-over. Second, the speaker is the victim himself, and he speaks twenty-two years later. This sentence has never been given to bystanders to stop a suffering person's mouth with. Remember that at the tomb of Lazarus the Lord Jesus wept first, and only afterwards performed the miracle.
4. The Coffin That Was Never Buried
The last five verses of Genesis are the most haunting ending in the whole book.
"Joseph lived in Egypt, he, and his father's house. Joseph lived one hundred ten years."
A hundred and ten years was, to the ancient Egyptian mind, the perfect lifespan.
"Joseph said to his brothers, 'I am dying, but God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.'" (Genesis 50:24)
"God will surely visit you" is פָּקֹד יִפְקֹד (*paqod yifqod*) in the Hebrew, the infinitive absolute — "God will certainly, certainly visit."
And in Exodus 3:16, when Moses comes back to the children of Israel, the very first thing he is given to say is, "I have surely visited you." The same word.
"Joseph took an oath from the children of Israel, saying, 'God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.'" (Genesis 50:25)
And then comes the last sentence of the whole of Genesis:
"So Joseph died, being one hundred ten years old, and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt." (Genesis 50:26)
Brothers and sisters, a book that opens with "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" closes on a coffin in a foreign country that nobody has buried.
It looks like an ending in defeat. And I want to tell you that that coffin was a sermon which went on being preached for four hundred years.
Think about it: an unburied coffin, standing there. Every generation of Israelites walking past would ask, who is that?
And the father would answer: that is Joseph. He said he did not want to be buried here. He said he would wait — wait for the day God takes us home.
So what that coffin was saying is this: we do not belong here.

Four hundred years later, Exodus 13:19: "Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for he had made the children of Israel swear, saying, 'God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones away from here with you.'"
And forty years after that, in the last chapter of Joshua: "They buried the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, in Shechem."
He waited more than four hundred years, and at last he came home.
Hebrews 11 sums it up like this: "By faith Joseph, when his end was near, made mention of the departure of the children of Israel, and gave instructions concerning his bones."

Out of that whole life the Bible picks exactly one thing to stand for Joseph's faith — not the interpreting of dreams, not the office of vizier, not the refusal of temptation, not even the forgiving of his brothers. This one thing: he gave instructions that his bones were to travel with them.
To establish God's system is to drive in a stake for a day you will never see.
And one more thing. The last word of Genesis in Hebrew is בְּמִצְרָיִם (*b'Mitzrayim*), "in Egypt." And the first word of Exodus in Hebrew is a conjunction — "and."
Genesis is not a full stop. It is a comma.
A book that ends on an unburied coffin — isn't that too bleak a way to finish?

It looks like an ending in defeat, and in fact that coffin was a sermon which went on being preached for four hundred years. Think about it: an unburied coffin standing there, and every generation of Israelites walking past would ask, "who is that?" — and the father would answer: that is Joseph; he said he did not want to be buried here, he said he would wait for the day God takes us home. So what the coffin was saying is: we do not belong here. And his dying words were "God will surely visit you", which in Hebrew is the infinitive absolute; and in Exodus 3, when Moses comes back to the children of Israel, the very first word he is given to say is that same word. Genesis has not ended. It has simply stopped in the middle of waiting.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
This is the most quoted chapter in the whole of Genesis, and also the most misused. There are several places you have to be able to recognise.

The first distortion is using "God meant it for good" to dismiss someone who is still in the middle of suffering. Joseph said it himself, twenty-two years afterwards. Said on his behalf by a bystander, it turns cruel. The test is this: when the person in pain has heard you out, have they been accompanied, or have they been sent away?

The second distortion is preaching God's sovereignty in such a way that human evil no longer has to answer for itself. The same verse says plainly, "you meant evil against me." Evil is evil. Preach sovereignty alone and the offender's responsibility is wiped off the books. The test is this: when the congregation has heard you out, is sin still sin?

The third distortion is preaching forgiveness as something that requires no repentance from the other side. Joseph watched them for two chapters and made sure they had changed before he made himself known; forgiveness is not the same as refusing to discern. Blur the two and the congregation will be told to walk back into dangerous relationships. Forgiveness can be a decision made by one side alone; reconciliation takes movement from both.

The fourth distortion is preaching the ending of Genesis as an ending in defeat. That coffin was not buried; it was waiting. And the first word of Exodus is a conjunction. Preach it as a full stop and the congregation will never see the comma. The test is this: the last picture your sermon leaves behind — is it the coffin standing in Egypt, or is it the empty tomb?

The fifth distortion is preaching "am I in the place of God?" as though it meant that nothing needs dealing with and everything can simply be left to God. Immediately after that same sentence, what Joseph did was to "provide for you and your little ones", and to speak kindly to them. Leaving it to God is not the same as doing nothing; what it means is: I will not sit in the judgement seat, but I will go on loving all the same.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: we find it very hard to believe that we have already been pardoned. We have believed for many years, we have confessed our sins many times, and still there is a corner of the heart that suspects God is probably keeping a record of that one thing. The brothers were still waiting for the reckoning seventeen years on. Brothers and sisters, that unease is not humility; it is unbelief — not believing that the pardon is real. This week, ask yourself one question: "Do I believe that I have already been forgiven?" Write the answer down. And if the answer is "not really", then read 1 John 1:9 ten times over: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." He said it, and that settles it.

The second question: when we comfort people, we get to the doctrine far too quickly. Somebody in the family dies and we say, "he is better off in heaven now." Somebody loses a job and we say, "God must have something better prepared." Somebody loses a child and we say, "God meant it for good." Every one of those things may be true, and said too early they simply pack a person's pain away in a hurry. The Lord Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus. This week, go and sit with somebody who is still down in the pit, and do not explain God's good purposes yet. All you have to do is sit down, listen to them, and be sad alongside them.
7. Living 321 Out — That Seat Is Not Mine
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Joseph said, "am I in the place of God?", and then went on to feed the very men who had harmed him. And the Lord Jesus said from the cross, "Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing." My role model is this: he held all authority, and he used that authority to forgive.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "once I feel I have let it go, then we'll talk"; the standard is "For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." Forgiveness is a decision, and the feelings come limping along behind.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to make yourself known, when simply to sit with someone, when the words "God meant it for good" may finally be spoken — all of that needs guidance. To rely on our intellect and lean on ourselves ends in worry: you will be in a hurry to get the matter explained and closed. To rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit ends in gladness: he knows whether what this person needs right now is words, or silence.

Let Jesus be King. "Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay." Refusing to forgive is, at bottom, insisting on sitting in the judgement seat. To let Jesus be King is to move that case out of my courtroom and into his — and you will find that the moment the file leaves your hands, your hands are free.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. What Joseph said was, "God meant it for good, to save many people alive." He was vizier for eighty years, and when he came to sum up his own life, what he talked about was what God had done.

Establish God's system. "You shall carry up my bones from here." A man who never saw the promise left a marker for people four hundred years down the line. To establish God's system is to drive in a stake for a day you cannot see; and if what you do with your life can only be seen by your own generation, it is not yet large enough.
What is the word they used for "forgive", and what does its meaning tell us?

The Hebrew is literally "please lift it up, please carry it away" — in Hebrew, to forgive is to shoulder something. And the two words they used for their offence are heavy ones: "disobedience" is the heaviest of the three Hebrew words for sin, meaning rebellion and treason, and "sin" has the root meaning "to miss the mark." They said the whole thing, and they said it properly — they simply said it through a messenger. And the meaning of that word tells us what forgiveness costs: forgiving is not striking a debt off the books, it is somebody carrying that debt away on their own back. Which is why everyone who has genuinely forgiven knows it was not a light thing — you shouldered the weight in the other person's place.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Coffin
We have read this book through with four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "I can forgive him, but he had better remember that he owes me." That is still sitting in the seat. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights — and refusing to forgive is the most respectable form of grabbing power there is; humility is returning to our position as human beings, saying "am I in the place of God?", and climbing down.

The fearful heart says, "If I really let go, what if he does it again?" Joseph's way was this: he discerned, and he made sure; and then he forgave, and provided. Forgiveness does not mean having no boundaries. You can let go and be wise at the same time.

The ashamed heart says, "I know he said he forgave me, but I don't dare believe it." So did the brothers. Seventeen years on. Brothers and sisters, if God has said you are pardoned and you go on convicting yourself, you are putting your own feelings above God's word. He said it, and that settles it.

The wounded heart says, "That sentence — 'God meant it for good' — I cannot say it right now." Then don't say it. It is a sentence spoken twenty-two years afterwards. God is not hurrying you. He let Joseph wait twenty-two years, and he will wait for you too. What you can say right now may be no more than "Lord, this hurts" — and he understands that sentence perfectly well.
Four kinds of heart, and one and the same coffin standing in Egypt. And the day that coffin was waiting for really did come.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, towards God. Take one person you have been privately sentencing in your heart, and hand him back to God in prayer. Say this: "Lord, I am transferring this case to you."
Second, towards yourself. Ask the question, "Do I believe that I have already been forgiven?", write the answer down honestly, and then bring it before God.
Third, towards other people. Sit with somebody who is still down in the pit. This week, do not explain God's good purposes; just sit down and listen until they have finished.

Fourth, towards daily living. Stop bringing up a matter you have already said you were letting go of. Not once — not at the dinner table, not in the group chat, and not on the loop that plays inside your own head.

Fifth, towards the calling. Do one thing whose fruit you will never see in your lifetime and which the next generation will ask about. It might be writing down your testimony, it might be raising up one young person, it might be beginning to pray regularly for one particular thing.

Sixth, tell a friend outside the church, in three sentences. First sentence: the last picture in the first book of the Bible is a coffin standing in a foreign land, unburied. Second sentence: the man in it left instructions as he died — on the day God takes you home, carry my bones with you. Third sentence: four hundred years later they really did carry him out with them — and that is why I believe that when God has said a thing, he does not forget it.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that the judgement seat is not mine; am I in the place of God?
I declare that I believe I have already been forgiven; he said it, and that settles it.
I declare that I will sit with people first and explain afterwards, as my Lord wept first at the tomb.
I declare that I will drive in a stake for a day I cannot yet see; what I do with this life is not for my generation alone.
Once the pardon has been announced, is the matter finished?

No. Verse 21 says, "'Now therefore don't be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.' He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them." That phrase "spoke kindly" is, in the Hebrew, "he spoke to their heart" — precisely the phrase of chapter 34, and the phrase behind what God says in Hosea: "I will allure her … and speak tenderly to her." He does not simply announce a pardon; he walks over and speaks to their heart. That is forgiveness made whole: the position is settled, and the feelings are cared for as well. A great many reconciliations are only half done, because only the first half was ever attempted.
Genesis has run its course. From "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" to "in a coffin in Egypt."
Fifty chapters, and in them a garden, a flood, a tower, tents, wells, a pit, a prison, a throne — and at the end, a coffin nobody buried.
And from beginning to end this book has been saying one thing: man keeps grabbing, God keeps giving; man keeps falling, God keeps coming after him.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because the One that coffin standing in Egypt was waiting for is precisely the God who "will surely visit"; and he did come in the end — and not only to bring a people out of Egypt, but to come right down into our death and to lie in a grave in our place. Except that on the third day, that grave was empty.

The word in chapter 3, that the offspring of the woman "will bruise your head"; the word in chapter 49, "The scepter will not depart from Judah"; and in chapter 50, this coffin waiting to go home — all of them point to the same person.
Genesis is not a full stop. It is a comma.

May God bless every one of us: to climb down out of the judgement seat; to believe that we really have been forgiven; to weep first and speak afterwards when we come alongside people who are hurting; to drive in a stake for the day we cannot yet see — until the One who is coming again gathers us and carries us home together. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.

This is the last lesson of the whole book, so leave an extra ten minutes for a review of the whole journey: ask each person to say one sentence — "the sentence I remember most from these fifty lessons."
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ Forgiveness does not say you were never in the wrong; it says the judgement seat is not mine. Is there a case still sitting in your own courtroom?
2. ★★ "What you meant" and "what God meant" have to be said together. What goes wrong when either half is missing?
3. ★ He did not simply announce a pardon; he "spoke to their heart". Which half of your own reconciliation have you finished?
4. ★★ That unburied coffin was saying, "we do not belong here." What is there in your daily living that says the same thing?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I am entitled to judge him), fearful (I don't dare believe I have really been forgiven), ashamed (what I did seventeen years ago is still weighing on me), wounded (the love I gave was taken for gritted teeth). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Don't be afraid, for am I in the place of God?" Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Who is the person in your heart whose case has never been closed? What price are you waiting for him to pay?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "I am going to climb down out of the judgement seat and hand so-and-so over to God."
9. ★★ This week, to whom will you "speak to the heart" — not merely forgiving, but walking over to comfort them? Give the name and say how.

Leader's reminder: never use "God meant it for good" to hurry anybody into forgiving. If someone is not yet ready, affirm their honesty. Sit with them first, and speak afterwards; that order cannot be reversed.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell the whole of Genesis to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First sentence: this book begins with "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth" and ends on a coffin standing in a foreign land, unburied. Second sentence: the man in that coffin was sold by his own brothers, and in the end he said to them, "am I in the place of God?" — he chose not to sit in the judgement seat. Third sentence: and that is why I believe what this book is saying — that man fails all the way through, and God is faithful all the way through. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the case you are handing over, and the sentence you remember most from these fifty lessons. Then pray for each other, giving thanks to the Lord for bringing us through all fifty chapters of Genesis, and asking him to make us remember all our lives: this is what people meant, but God meant it for good.
